chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
title: Finding rooms in the South
summary: Accommodations were rough, and bands stayed in poor hotels or private homes; Armstrong kept contacts who saved him rooms.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Now, what about in the South? Wasn't it hard with accommodations?

Yeah, accommodations were very hard. Most of the time, if there wasn't a flea-bitten hotel you stayed in, you had to stay with private families. You'd go around from door to door, knocking on the door; you know, ask people if they got rooms or something like that. It was very tough, very tough.

Well, see, Louis had been all over the territory so many times before, he knew where he was going. See, any time you find a good place, you remember that, you know, and keep in contact with them people a few days before you're comin' into town. Or if you're a good roomer with them, they will remember you, and they see the advertisement that Louis is coming into town, they will save a room for you -- they'll save you a room.
